title: Pyramid Transition Matrix
statement:
You want to stack lettered blocks into a pyramid whose lowest row is exactly the string `bottom`. Every row above has one block fewer than the row under it, and each of its blocks rests on two neighbouring blocks of that lower row: the block at position `i` sits on positions `i` and `i + 1`.

A placement is legal only if it matches a pattern in `allowed`. Each pattern is a three-letter string `XYZ` meaning block `Z` may sit on top of the pair with `X` on the left and `Y` on the right; the order matters, so `"ABC"` does not permit `C` on top of `B` (left) and `A` (right).

Return `true` if some choice of blocks completes the pyramid up to a single block at the top using only legal placements, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: Every letter in bottom and allowed is one of 'A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E', 'F'
The strings in allowed are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Each level is decided entirely by the level under it, so the question is whether some sequence of choices reaches a single block. That is a search: build the row above one block at a time, and whenever a position has no legal block, back up and try the next option. Two ideas keep it fast. A hash map from each two-letter base to its possible tops makes every choice a direct lookup, and a set of rows already shown to be dead ends stops the search from rebuilding the same doomed row along a different route. The brute force lists every possible next row up front and recurses with no memory.

## Approach

1. Build `tops`, mapping each base `pair` such as `"BC"` to the list of letters allowed on it.
2. `solve(row)` returns `true` at a single block, `false` for a row in `failed`, and otherwise asks `fill(row, '')`, recording the row in `failed` if that fails.
3. `fill(row, next)` grows the row above: once `next` is one shorter than `row` it is complete, so recurse with `solve(next)`.
4. Otherwise take the `pair` under the next position and try each `block` in its `options`, returning `true` as soon as one leads to a finished pyramid.
5. If no option works, return `false` so the caller tries its next choice.

## Example 1, step by step

`bottom = "BCD"`, so `tops` is `BC → [C]`, `CD → [E]`, `CE → [A]`, `FF → [F]`. Filling above `"BCD"`: pair `"BC"` gives `next = "C"`, pair `"CD"` gives `"CE"`. That row is complete, so `solve("CE")` fills above it: pair `"CE"` gives `"A"`, and `solve("A")` reaches a single block, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: exponential in the worst case. With A = 6 letters, a row of length L has at most A^(L-1) candidate rows above it, and `failed` makes each distinct row expand at most once, so the work is bounded by about A^(2n-3) for `n = bottom.length`; with `n <= 6` and early exits this stays small.
- Space: O(A^(n-1)) for the remembered dead-end rows, plus O(n²) recursion depth.

## Pitfalls

- Patterns are ordered: `"ABC"` and `"BAC"` are different bases.
- Without `failed`, the same row can be rebuilt again and again through different routes, and dense inputs that end in `false` become very slow.
- With an empty `allowed` the answer is always `false`, since `bottom` has at least two blocks.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tops` | base pair → letters that may sit on it |
| `failed` | rows already proven unable to reach the top |
| `row` | the row currently being built on |
| `next` | the partly built row above `row` |
| `pair`, `options` | the two blocks under the next position and the letters allowed there |
| `block` | the letter being tried |

narration.2: Map each two-block base to the letters that may sit on it.
narration.3: Go through every allowed pattern once.
narration.4: The first two letters are the base pair, left then right.
narration.6: The third letter is a block allowed on top of that pair.
narration.8: Rows already proven unable to reach the top.
narration.10: A single block is the tip: the pyramid is finished.
narration.11: This row was explored before and failed, so do not repeat the work.
narration.12: Try to build some row above this one that leads to the top.
narration.13: Every choice failed, so remember this row as a dead end.
narration.17: The row above is complete, so try to build on it in turn.
narration.18: Look at the two blocks under the next position to fill.
narration.19: Fetch the letters allowed on that pair, or none.
narration.20: Try each allowed letter in turn.
narration.21: Place it and keep filling; stop as soon as one choice reaches the top.
narration.23: No letter here works, so back up and let the caller try its next choice.
narration.25: Start the search from the given bottom row.
